models.purpose: Size the network from a capturing radius.
models.summary: A full charge covers about 300 miles, so the capturing radius is capped at 15 miles, leaving 5 percent of charge on arrival. The radius shrinks with density and income: ru = cu / (rho v G)^(1/4) and rs = cs / (rho v G)^(1/4), both at most 15 miles. cu is fit to the finished Manhattan network. Stations per 40-mile square equal the ceiling of 40 squared over r squared. Rural roads get a station every 20 miles, and a village under 10,000 people gets one. The US total is 130,433 stations: 58,739 urban, 42,533 suburban, 29,161 rural. Expressway stations are 90 percent superchargers; urban and village stations are 70 percent destination chargers. Korea gets 30,343 superchargers, with destination radii of 5, 10 and 15 km.

models.purpose: Date the switch with a logistic curve.
models.summary: The Tesla share grows as dR/dt = k R, then capped as dR/dt = k R (1 - R), giving R = C exp(kt) / (1 + C exp(kt)) with C = 0.01 from a 1 percent share in 2018. The rate k is 0.3 urban, 0.26 suburban and 0.22 rural. South Korea reaches 10 percent by the end of 2026, 30 by 2031, 50 by 2034 and 90 by 2042. The fleet at those dates is 2.246, 2.250, 2.253 and 2.276 million. Total vehicles follow dy/dt = 2.2e-4 (5000 - y) against a population of fifty million.

models.purpose: Decide whether a country can build the network.
models.summary: Countries are gridded by GDP per capita, cut at 3,000 and 10,000 USD, and by population density, cut at 100 and 300 per square mile. A country below 3,000 USD is told not to switch yet. A country larger than 1,000 square miles with a Gini above 0.6 is split into parts and each part is classed on its own. Feasibility uses f(x) = a x + b - p + c exp(kx): build only when profit exceeds cost, and the stagnation point dates the first affordable year. China passes; Indonesia does not.
